en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Venerable Aniruddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, and the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa.
Translated by the subject Shi Hu and others, by imperial decree: Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a community of bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a venerable one named Aniruddha who, in the vicinity of Rājagṛha, was walking alone in meditation within a great monastic dwelling atop a solitary peak in the Śītavana charnel ground where snakes gathered.
Suddenly, he was bitten by a venomous snake; the serpent’s body was thin and slender with a brilliant luster, fierce and terrifying, like an añjana-śarāka.
Immediately, the Venerable Anuvīrya called out to the assembly of bhikṣus, saying: "Venerable sirs!
I have been bitten by a venomous snake; my flesh and body are溃烂 (corrupted). You should now place me outside the monastery so that the poison does not spread further."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was sitting under a tree not far from where the Venerable Aniruddha was staying. Hearing those words spoken by Aniruddha, he immediately went to him.
Upon arrival, he said: "Venerable Aniruddha!
"I have observed your face and your faculties; they were originally without any signs of change. For what reason do you now utter such a sound?
Suyodhana replied, "Venerable One!"
"I have been bitten by a venomous snake; my flesh and body are溃烂 (corrupted and festering). You should now place me outside the monastery so that the poison does not spread further."
“Venerable Śāriputra!
If I were to grasp at them, [I would think: ‘The eye is mine; the eye is my possession.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are mine; the mind is my possession.’”
Form is self; form is mine.
Sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena are self; mental phenomena are mine.
The earth element is self; the earth element is mine.
The element of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness is my self; the element of consciousness is mine.
The aggregate of form is my self; the aggregate of form is mine.
The aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are my self; the aggregate of consciousness is mine.
"If I were to grasp at such dharmas as these, my face and my sense faculties would exhibit some sign of change.
Venerable Śāriputra!
I do not grasp at dharmas in this way, saying: 'The eye is the self; the eye belongs to the self.'"
"Up to the aggregate of consciousness, it is 'I,' and the aggregate of consciousness is 'mine.
Now, for what reason do the face and the various sense organs have these differing characteristics?
Śāriputra replied:
“Venerable Ānanda!

If one has already severed attachment by abandoning views of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ as well as the conceit ‘I am,’ and furthermore understands that the root of what was severed is forever cut off without remainder—just as the heart of a tāla tree is destroyed so that it never grows again—and has realized the dharma of non-arising, how could there be any further distinct characteristics to be found in such a person?”
Then the Venerable Śāriputra placed the Venerable Svāgata outside the monastery and he collapsed prostrate on the ground.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra spoke these verses:
“The wise one practices the holy life well, And constantly cultivates the causes of the noble path.”
When the time of passing away approaches, joy arises in the heart, like a gravely ill person recovering from a light illness.

The wise one who practices the holy life well and constantly cultivates the causes of the Noble Path experiences joy when the time of passing away approaches, as if casting away a vessel of foul poison.
The wise one practices the holy life well, and constantly cultivates the causes of the right path;
thus, at the time of relinquishing the retribution of existence, they emerge with brilliant liberation, like a person escaping from a house of fire.
Wise ones practice the holy life and cultivate the right path;
they view the entire world as mere grass and wood, seeing that it is utterly devoid of benefit or achievement, and ultimately remain entirely unattached.

At that time, after the Venerable Śāriputra had attended to the needs of the Venerable Aniruddha, he went to where the Buddha was. Upon arrival, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One and reported the aforementioned matter in detail.
The Buddha said,

"Śāriputra! If that noble son Anuvīrya should at that time hear me recite these sublime verses and the great mantra syllables, he will certainly not be bitten by the venomous snake, nor will his body be destroyed."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are these most excellent and sublime verses?”
"What are these great mantras and phrases?
I pray that you will explain them to me.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Dhṛtarāṣṭra, King of the Devas, practices loving-kindness; so too does the Naga Elāpattra.
Aśvatara, Kambala, and Śvetapāda—all of them are filled with loving-kindness.”
I practice loving-kindness, O Virūpākṣa Devaputra; the black Gopaka dragon practices loving-kindness likewise.
Nanda and Upananda, those two dragons, practice loving-kindness in the same way.

I practice loving-kindness toward those without feet; likewise for those with two feet and four feet, as well as for all sentient beings with many feet—I practice this mind of loving-kindness equally, without any distinction.

All the nāgas and others practice loving-kindness; those nāgas dwell within the great ocean, maintaining a mind of universal compassion toward all sentient beings, whether in their mental states or their physical forms.
May all classes of sentient beings, down to the smallest flying insects and crawling worms,
universally find the causes of illness and affliction eliminated, and may they all attain peace and happiness; may all classes of sentient beings,
down to the smallest flying insects and crawling worms, [attain peace and happiness].
Universally viewing all with virtuous equanimity, I have cleansed away every evil and transgression.
Though the venom of serpents is most fierce and blazing, and their poison can destroy a person’s life,
yet within those serpent caves upon mountain peaks, I dwell constantly and roam above them.
I am the unsurpassed teacher of the world; I always proclaim words of truth.
By the power of my karma of truthful speech, the venom of snakes cannot enter my body.
All phenomena of greed, hatred, and delusion—these three are the great poisons of the world.
The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One is not invaded by poison; the Buddha’s true power can destroy all poison.
All phenomena of greed, hatred, and delusion—these three are the great poisons of the world.
The World-Honored One’s True Dharma is not invaded by poison; The true power of the Dharma can destroy all poisons.
All phenomena of greed, hatred, and delusion— These are the great poisons of the three worlds.
The World-Honored One’s pure assembly is not invaded by poison; The true power of the Sangha can destroy all poisons.
Among all the poisons that exist in the world, the poison of greed is the most supreme;
only the Buddha can destroy it and hold it in check, whereby all poisons are utterly extinguished.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this Great Mantra:

*Tadyathā:* 1. *Oṃ* 2. *Dumili* 3. *Dumili* 4. *Dumi* 5. *Pradumi* 6. *Nati* 7. *Sunati* 8. *Gīrvati* 9. *Munaye* 10. *Sāmāye* 11. *Nande* 12. *Nandili* 13. *Nirli* 14. *Niragīśi* 15. *Vāri* 16. *Varāgīśi* 17. *Ulli* 18. *Niryāgūri svāhā* The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra!
Ananda, son of noble family!
If at that time one should hear me recite these verses and the syllables of the great mantra, they will certainly not be bitten by snake venom nor have their bodies destroyed.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding these sublime and wondrous verses and this great vidyā-mantra spoken by the Buddha just now—when that Bhikṣu Anuvīrya was bitten by the snake, he was far removed from the Buddha’s presence; how then could he have obtained such a wondrous Dharma?”
At that time, having spoken these words, the Venerable Śāriputra prostrated with his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from the assembly of the Buddha.
This concludes the *Bhagavān-bhāṣita-Aniruddha-sūtra*.
